extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, logicians, and advanced students concerned with induction, classification, and the theory of definition
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for constructing, naming, and refining general conceptions (classes/definitions) that support valid induction and scientific inquiry; includes standards for clarity, appropriateness, definition, and the use of language as an instrument of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of a conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception must correspond to a real agreement among the phenomena and be appropriate to the particular object or purpose in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriateness is relative to the problem: a conception that groups objects by trivial or irrelevant commonalities (e.g., color) may be legitimate but not appropriate to another purpose (e.g., understanding structure or mode of life). An appropriate conception should include agreements that lead to important, informative consequences about the phenomenon studied; inappropriate conceptions either miss important points of agreement or include agreements irrelevant to the law sought (examples: Aristotle's 'toward its own place' for spontaneous motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (determinate conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear conception is one in which we know exactly in what the agreement consists; it is carefully observed, accurately remembered, and determinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague, fluctuating, or merely felt resemblances. A clear conception implies that one can state the specific properties by which the class is constituted, never varies (except by conscious revision), and is not one thing today and another tomorrow. Attainment of clarity requires attentive observation, extensive experience, and accurate memory; do not class items unless you can state why they are so classed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must correspond to real classes (real distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The class framed must be a real class: the things it includes must really agree with one another in certain particulars and differ from other things in those same particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a name groups things that lack common properties (or properties common also to other things), general truths applicable to that class cannot be ascertained. A 'person without clear ideas' habitually classes disparate things together or cannot state the common properties that justify a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select properties in definitions that serve the purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes and definitions should be formed by selecting properties that are of primary importance for the theoretical or practical purpose at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer properties that 'go deepest into the nature of the things' for theoretical aims, or those most closely connected with the particular property under investigation. Example contrast: classing animals by skeleton structure vs. color—one is more informative for understanding structure and habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid permanent acquiescence in premature conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions formed prematurely (Bacon's 'notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ') impede progress when they are accepted permanently without revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form provisional conceptions as working hypotheses but be ready to alter them as knowledge advances. The mind necessarily forms imperfect conceptions in progress; harm occurs when one refuses to exchange badly made classes for better ones discovered later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior conceptions and hypotheses as investigative aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering the important agreement among phenomena sometimes requires invoking conceptions or hypotheses acquired elsewhere (scientific imagination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When straightforward comparison fails to reveal the unifying attribute, call upon imagination to propose possible resemblances or 'places' to search; success often depends on having a store of related conceptions and the faculty to recombine known elements into plausible hypotheses (example: planetary orbits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and general names as instruments of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: General names and language are necessary instruments for carrying inductive inference beyond the simplest particulars because they record, transmit, and recall uniformities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without general names, reasoning from past experience to new cases would be limited; words serve as an 'artificial memory' making complex comparisons, experiments, and communications possible. General names register uniformities once ascertained and serve as formulas for applying inductive inferences to individual cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every general name should have a fixed and precisely determined meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: For names to perform their function in investigation, each general name must have a steadily fixed connotation—its meaning must be knowable and precise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meaning of a connotative general name resides in the attribute(s) it denotes; definitions must fix the connotation so that propositions involving the name can be tested by induction. Vague common usage undermines inductive tests and communication of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain existing connotation before redefining
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a term already in use, determine and, as far as possible, preserve the associations and propositions already connected with that name rather than arbitrarily assigning a new meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not clash with established usage in ways that render generally received propositions false; the fixed connotation should agree (as far as it goes) with the vague connotation the term already has. Radical redefinition that contradicts entrenched propositions is impractical and undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for giving a good definition of an existing name
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a concrete general name, analyze the particular attributes common to the objects it denotes and select from among them those properties which are sure marks or on which many other properties depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First ascertain, by comparison (and sometimes induction), the common attributes of the denoted objects. Then choose attributes for the connotation that are well known, serve as causes or marks of other properties, and best distinguish the class from others. Definitions demand discussion of both usage and the properties/causes of things; they improve as scientific theory improves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and concept-explication must be grounded in the properties of things
rubrics_metrics.description: The explication of conceptions (unfolding what the general conception consists in) is not merely linguistic but depends on ascertaining the real properties of the things classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversies of definition become significant only because they presuppose propositions the definition is meant to express; accordingly, disputes about definitions are substantive questions about truth (examples: definitions of force, heat, chemical combination). Definitions should thus rest on empirical or deductive understanding of the subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely vague/common-language connotations when testing by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions that cannot be precisely stated because the underlying name lacks a fixed connotation cannot have been brought to the test of correct induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like 'civilized', 'honor', or 'gentleman' often carry loose, varying connotations; such vagueness must be resolved by analyzing what propositions are actually predicated of the term before using it in inductive testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological requisites for good conceptions: observation, comparison, memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits of attentive observation, frequent and careful comparison, and accurate memory are principal requisites for forming clear and appropriate conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearness depends chiefly on carefulness and accuracy of observation/comparison; appropriateness depends on activity and readiness in these faculties. Those trained to observe and compare will more readily perceive important agreements and thus are likelier to hit upon appropriate conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part structure of induction and the role of general propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction consists in (1) ascertaining what is a mark of the given fact and (2) checking for that mark in new cases; general propositions summarize uniformities and make the second step practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when a single-case inference can be made without general propositions, complex inductive work requires general names/propositions to remember and apply uniformities across varying circumstances; language enables this division and preserves results for future application.
